summary:
ANALOG FINDER is a web app that ranks 30 places on Earth by how closely they resemble the Moon and Mars. It’s built for mission planners, rover teams and students who need somewhere on Earth to test before launch.

A logistic-regression model is trained on 30 labelled sites (15 good analogs, 15 poor). It scores each place from environmental measurements: solar exposure, temperature swing, slope, rainfall, vegetation, albedo and terrain roughness. The results appear on an interactive 3D globe beside the Moon and Mars. Each score comes with the factors behind it, how the model did when that site was held out, and the most similar known sites. This answers the challenge’s question directly. It turns a few hand-picked analog sites into a repeatable, explainable method that can score any place on Earth. It matters because analog testing is expensive and the choice of site is still mostly expert judgment. We report leave-one-out accuracy of 87% (95% interval 73 to 97%) and state plainly that most of the signal comes from vegetation and rainfall. It is a screening tool, not a verdict.
details:
ANALOG FINDER ranks 30 places on Earth by how closely they resemble the Moon and Mars. A ridge-regularised logistic-regression model is trained on 30 labelled sites: 15 good analogs, such as Atacama, Haughton Crater and Makhtesh Ramon, and 15 poor ones, such as rainforests, cities and farmland. It uses 16 environmental inputs, including solar exposure, temperature swing, slope, rainfall, aridity, wind, terrain roughness (TRI/TWI), surface albedo, insolation and vegetation (NDVI). Each site appears on an interactive 3D globe next to the Moon and Mars. The app shows the probability that the site is a good analog, which inputs pushed that score up or down, and the most similar known sites. Every score is a held-out score: it comes from a model that never saw that site.

Benefits. It turns analog-site selection, which is mostly expert judgment today, into a transparent and repeatable method. Students, small rover and habitat teams and educators can shortlist test sites worldwide, not just the famous few, and see exactly why a site scores the way it does.

Intended impact. Cheaper, faster, better-justified choices of where to rehearse Moon and Mars missions on Earth. It also gives the public an explorable way to learn why terrain and climate matter in planetary exploration.

Tools and technologies. The stack is PostgreSQL (Neon), Express 5 and Node.js 22, with a React 19 front end built on Next.js (the PERN stack), written in JavaScript and TypeScript. Model analysis and checks used Python and scikit-learn. The globe uses NASA and JAXA Moon and Mars imagery via NASA Trek. The project has automated tests for the API and the model. It is deployed on Vercel, and Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code, testing and documentation.

Creativity. Instead of a black-box score, every prediction is explained input by input and compared with its nearest known analogs, side by side with the actual Moon and Mars. The app also runs fully in the browser if the server is down.

Factors we considered. With only 30 labelled sites, we chose a simple, explainable model and validated it with leave-one-out testing. It reaches 87% held-out accuracy , and most of the signal comes from vegetation and rainfall, so we present it as a screening tool, not a verdict. We also flagged data issues openly, including some site coordinates and duplicated values, and built in security protections and a no-server fallback for reliability.
